title: The Coordinate Plane and Patterns
bigQuestion: How can two numbers tell you exactly where something is, and what does a pattern look like when you graph it?

story.title: The X at (7, 4)
story.kicker: A treasure map with no trees, no rivers and no landmarks, only a grid and one pair of numbers.
paragraphs: On the last day of camp, the counselor hands each cabin a folded map. There are no trees, no rivers and no big rocks drawn on it. There is only a grid of squares, numbers along the bottom edge, numbers up the left edge, and a note: the X is at (7, 4).

Jamal's cabin argues. Does 7 mean seven steps up or seven steps over? Priya says the first number always means across, because you read a map the way you read a sentence, left to right first. They start at the corner where both edges read 0. They count 7 squares to the right, then 4 squares up, and put a finger on that spot.

Another cabin starts at the same corner, counts 4 to the right and 7 up, and digs in the wrong place. The order of the numbers matters. (7, 4) and (4, 7) are two different spots on the map. The corner where the numbers start, the point (0, 0), is where every trip begins.

Jamal's cabin paces it out in the field. Each square on the map is 10 steps. They walk 70 steps east and 40 steps north and find a box of snacks under a flat stone. On the way back, Priya notices something. Her count of steps makes a pattern: 10, 20, 30, 40. Numbers that grow by the same amount each time make a straight row of dots when you plot them. The grid is not just for treasure. It is a way to draw any pattern.
story.think: Why does the order of the two numbers in (7, 4) matter? What could go wrong if a map did not say which number comes first?

lessons.title: Ordered Pairs
lessons.mainIdea: An ordered pair (x, y) tells you first how far to go right, then how far to go up, starting from (0, 0).
reading: A *coordinate plane* is a grid made by two number lines that cross at a right angle. The line going across is the *x-axis*. The line going up is the y-axis. They cross at a point called the *origin*, labeled (0, 0). In this chapter we use only the part of the grid where both numbers are 0 or bigger. That part is called the first quadrant.

Every point on the grid has an address made of two numbers, called an *ordered pair*. The first number is the x-coordinate: how many units to move right from the origin. The second number is the y-coordinate: how many units to move up. To find (3, 5), start at the origin, move 3 right, then 5 up. Say it as 'over 3, up 5'. The x comes first, just as x comes before y in the alphabet.

The order is the whole point. (3, 5) and (5, 3) are different spots. (3, 5) is over 3 and up 5. (5, 3) is over 5 and up 3. Common mistake: reading the y first because the y-axis stands up tall. Another: mixing up points on the axes. (4, 0) sits on the x-axis, 4 units right and 0 up. (0, 4) sits on the y-axis, 0 right and 4 up. The origin, (0, 0), is where you always begin.

words.d: a grid made by two number lines, the x-axis and the y-axis, crossing at a right angle
the number line that runs across the coordinate plane; the first number in a pair is measured along it
the point (0, 0) where the two axes cross; every count starts there
two numbers in order, (x, y), that name one point: over x, then up y

look.title: Two Cabins, Two Spots
look.text: Cabin A reads the note (7, 4) as over 7, up 4. Cabin B reads it as over 4, up 7. Both start at the origin. Cabin A ends 7 units right and 4 units up. Cabin B ends 4 units right and 7 units up. On the grid, Cabin A's spot is farther to the right and lower. Cabin B's spot is farther to the left and higher.
look.prompt: Which cabin read the ordered pair correctly? How far apart, going across, are the two spots? How far apart going up?

check.q: To plot (2, 6), start at the origin and
check.why: The first number is x (right), the second is y (up): right 2, up 6.

check.q: Which point lies on the x-axis?
check.why: A point on the x-axis has gone up 0, so its y-coordinate is 0: (5, 0).

check.q: What is the ordered pair for the origin?
check.why: The origin is where the axes cross, with no movement right or up: (0, 0).

lessons.title: Plotting and Naming Points
lessons.mainIdea: To name a point, read straight down to the x-axis first, then straight across to the y-axis.
reading: To *plot* is to go from numbers to a dot. To name is to go from a dot to numbers. To name a point, put your finger on it. Slide straight down to the x-axis and read that number: the x-coordinate. Go back to the point and slide straight left to the y-axis: the y-coordinate. Write them as (x, y). A dot that is 6 over and 2 up is named (6, 2).

Plot these four points and connect them in order: A (1, 1), B (5, 1), C (5, 4), D (1, 4), then back to A. A and B are both 1 up, so segment AB is flat, or *horizontal*. B and C are both 5 over, so BC goes straight up; it is *vertical*. The shape is a rectangle, 4 units wide and 3 units tall. Points that share a y-coordinate make a horizontal segment. Points that share an x-coordinate make a vertical segment.

Common mistakes when naming: counting the grid lines instead of the spaces, or starting the count at 1 instead of 0. The origin is 0, and the first line to the right of it is 1. Another mistake: reading a label above the point instead of below it. Always trace down to the x-axis first. Then trace left to the y-axis.

words.d: to mark a point on the grid from its ordered pair
running across, level with the x-axis, like the horizon
running straight up and down, like the y-axis

look.title: Corners of a Rectangle
look.cite: Points A, B and C from the reading
look.prompt: Point D is straight above A and straight left of C. What are its coordinates? How wide and how tall is the rectangle ABCD?

check.q: A dot is 3 units right of the origin and 7 units up. Its name is
check.why: Right comes first, then up: (3, 7).

check.q: Points (2, 5) and (9, 5) are connected. The segment is
check.why: The same y-coordinate means the same height, so the segment runs flat across.

check.q: When naming a point, what do you read first?
choices: the number to its left on the y-axis
the number straight below it on the x-axis
check.why: The x-coordinate comes first, and you find it by tracing straight down to the x-axis.

lessons.title: Distances Along the Grid
lessons.mainIdea: If two points share a coordinate, the distance between them is the difference of the other coordinates.
reading: How far is it from (2, 3) to (9, 3)? Both points are 3 up, so they sit on the same horizontal line. Count the squares between them, or just subtract the x-coordinates: 9 − 2 = 7 units. Now try (4, 1) to (4, 10). Same x, so the points are on a vertical line. Subtract the y-coordinates: 10 − 1 = 9 units. The *distance* is the *difference* of the coordinates that are not the same.

For a trip that turns a corner, add the legs. From (1, 2) go to (6, 2), then up to (6, 8). First leg: 6 − 1 = 5. Second leg: 8 − 2 = 6. Total: 5 + 6 = 11 units. On a city grid, this is how far you walk when you cannot cut through buildings. If each unit is one block, that trip is 11 blocks.

Common mistake: subtracting the wrong pair. From (2, 3) to (9, 3), a student computes 9 − 3 = 6, mixing an x with a y. Always subtract x from x or y from y. Another mistake: counting grid lines instead of spaces, which gives one too many. From 2 to 9 there are 7 spaces, not 8. Check with a tiny case: from 2 to 3 is 1 space, and 3 − 2 = 1.

words.d: how far apart two points are, measured in grid units
the answer to a subtraction; the larger coordinate minus the smaller one

look.title: Walking the Blocks
look.text: On a grid of city blocks, the library is at (3, 8) and the school is at (3, 2). A student walks from the school straight to the library. Both points have x = 3, so the walk is vertical: 8 − 2 = 6 blocks. After the library, the student walks to a park at (10, 8). Both of those points have y = 8, so this leg is horizontal.
look.prompt: How long is the second leg? How many blocks is the whole trip from the school to the park by way of the library?

check.q: What is the distance from (5, 6) to (5, 1)?
check.why: Same x, so subtract the y-coordinates: 6 − 1 = 5.

check.q: What is the distance from (1, 4) to (8, 4)?
check.why: Same y, so subtract the x-coordinates: 8 − 1 = 7.

check.q: A path goes from (0, 0) to (6, 0), then to (6, 5). How long is the whole path?
check.why: 6 + 5 = 11. Multiplying 6 × 5 would give an area, not a distance.

lessons.title: Graphing a Pattern
lessons.mainIdea: A pattern becomes a set of points when you pair each step number with its value.
reading: Marta saves $3 every week. After 1 week she has $3, after 2 weeks $6, after 3 weeks $9, after 4 weeks $12. Make a *table* with two columns: week and dollars. Now turn each row into an ordered pair: (1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9), (4, 12). Plot them, with weeks on the x-axis and dollars on the y-axis. The points march up in a straight line.

Why a straight line? Each step right (one more week) goes up the same amount (3 dollars). A *pattern* that adds the same number each time always plots as points in a straight line. The steeper the line, the bigger the number being added. Saving $5 a week would make a steeper line: (1, 5), (2, 10), (3, 15). Saving $1 a week would make a line that is nearly flat.

Read the graph backward too. A point at (6, 18) says: after 6 weeks, $18. To find the amount after 10 weeks, *extend* the pattern: 10 × 3 = 30, the point (10, 30). Common mistake: swapping the axes and plotting (3, 1) for week 1. Put the week first, because it is what you choose, and the dollars depend on it. Another mistake: drawing a solid line when only whole weeks make sense. Points are enough.

words.d: rows and columns of numbers; here, one column for the step and one for its value
a list of numbers made by a rule, like adding 3 each time
to continue a pattern past the numbers you were given

look.title: Marta's Savings
look.prompt: What ordered pair goes with week 8? If Marta wants $45, in which week does she reach it?

check.q: A pattern adds 4 each step, starting at 4. Which ordered pair belongs to it?
check.why: Step 3 has value 4 × 3 = 12, so the pair is (3, 12): step first, value second.

check.q: Which pattern makes the steepest line of points?
check.why: The bigger the amount added, the more each point rises, so adding 5 is steepest.

check.q: The point (7, 21) is on the graph of a savings pattern. What does it mean?
check.why: The x-coordinate is the week and the y-coordinate is the dollars: 7 weeks, $21.

lessons.title: Two Patterns Side by Side
lessons.mainIdea: When two patterns start at 0 and one adds twice as much, every value in the second is twice the matching value in the first.
reading: Start two patterns at 0. Pattern A adds 3 each step: 0, 3, 6, 9, 12. Pattern B adds 6 each step: 0, 6, 12, 18, 24. Line them up. Step 1: 3 and 6. Step 2: 6 and 12. Step 3: 9 and 18. Each B value is exactly double the *corresponding* A value. That makes sense. B adds twice as much every time, so after any number of steps B has twice as much.

Now graph the pairs (A, B): (0, 0), (3, 6), (6, 12), (9, 18). These points also fall in a straight line, and every point has a y that is twice its x. Try another pair. Pattern C adds 2: 0, 2, 4, 6. Pattern D adds 10: 0, 10, 20, 30. Each D value is 5 times the matching C value, because 10 is 5 times 2.

Common mistake: saying B is always 3 more than A. That is only true at step 1. At step 4, A is 12 and B is 24, a difference of 12, not 3. The *relationship* that stays true at every step is that B is 2 times A. Ask: what do I multiply A by to get B? If the patterns do not both start at 0, the rule is different, so check the starting numbers first.

words.d: matching; the values from two patterns that sit at the same step
a rule that connects the corresponding values of two patterns, like 'B is twice A'

look.title: Add 3 Versus Add 6
look.cite: Pattern A adds 3, pattern B adds 6, both starting at 0
look.prompt: What is A at step 10? What is B at step 10? What single rule connects every pair of values?

check.q: Pattern A adds 4 each step from 0. Pattern B adds 8 each step from 0. At step 5, what are A and B?
check.why: A: 4 × 5 = 20. B: 8 × 5 = 40, which is double.

check.q: Two patterns start at 0. One adds 2, the other adds 10. Each value in the second pattern is
check.why: 10 is 5 times 2, so at every step the second pattern has 5 times as much.

check.q: Which is true at every step for A (add 3) and B (add 6), both starting at 0?
check.why: At step 1 the values are 3 and 6; at step 4 they are 12 and 24. Only 'B is twice A' holds every time.

lessons.title: Rules That Add
lessons.mainIdea: An add rule tells you the start and what to add; to find any term, apply the rule step by step or count the jumps.
reading: A *rule* is an instruction that makes a pattern. 'Start at 5, add 4' gives 5, 9, 13, 17, 21. Each number is a *term*. The first term is 5. To get the next term, add 4. To find the 6th term, keep going: 21 + 4 = 25. Or count the jumps: five jumps of 4 after the start. 5 + 5 × 4 = 5 + 20 = 25. Either way, the 6th term is 25.

Rules can subtract too. 'Start at 50, subtract 7' gives 50, 43, 36, 29, 22. Check: 43 − 7 = 36, and 36 − 7 = 29. The terms go down by the same amount each time. To find a rule from a pattern, subtract neighbors. In 8, 14, 20, 26, each gap is the same: 14 − 8 = 6, 20 − 14 = 6, 26 − 20 = 6. Rule: start at 8, add 6.

Common mistakes: forgetting the start, so 'start at 5, add 4' turns into 4, 8, 12. Or adding one extra jump: the 6th term has 5 jumps after the first term, not 6. Count the jumps on your fingers. Term 1 to term 2 is one jump. Another mistake when finding a rule: subtracting in the wrong order. Later term minus earlier term gives the gap.

words.d: an instruction that makes a pattern: where to start and what to do each step
one number in a pattern; the 1st term is the start

look.title: The Stair Pattern
look.text: A staircase is built from blocks. Step 1 uses 4 blocks. Each new step uses 3 more blocks than the one before. So step 2 uses 7, step 3 uses 10 and step 4 uses 13. Rule: start at 4, add 3. To find step 8, count 7 jumps of 3 after the start: 4 + 7 × 3 = 4 + 21 = 25 blocks.
look.prompt: How many blocks does step 6 use? Which step uses exactly 34 blocks? Show the jumps.

check.q: Rule: start at 6, add 5. What is the 4th term?
check.why: 6, 11, 16, 21. Three jumps of 5 after 6: 6 + 15 = 21.

check.q: Pattern: 30, 26, 22, 18. What is the rule?
check.why: Each term is 4 less than the one before: 30 − 4 = 26, 26 − 4 = 22, 22 − 4 = 18.

check.q: Rule: start at 2, add 9. What is the 10th term?
check.why: Nine jumps after the start: 2 + 9 × 9 = 2 + 81 = 83.

lessons.title: Rules That Multiply
lessons.mainIdea: A multiply rule grows faster and faster, because each term is a multiple of the one before.
reading: 'Start at 1, multiply by 2' gives 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. Each term is *double* the one before. Compare that with 'start at 1, add 2', which gives 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11. The add pattern climbs steadily. The multiply pattern climbs slowly at first and then races ahead. By the 6th term, the doubling pattern is at 32 while the add pattern is at 11. Folding paper gets thick so fast for the same reason. Each fold doubles the layers.

To find a multiply rule from a pattern, divide neighbors. In 3, 12, 48, 192: 12 ÷ 3 = 4, 48 ÷ 12 = 4, 192 ÷ 48 = 4. Rule: start at 3, multiply by 4. Every term is a *multiple* of the one before it. Check the next term: 192 × 4 = 768. Rules can divide too. 'Start at 80, divide by 2' gives 80, 40, 20, 10, 5.

On a graph, an add pattern makes points in a straight line. A multiply pattern makes points that curve upward, getting steeper. Common mistake: testing only the first gap. In 2, 4, 8 a student sees 4 − 2 = 2 and says 'add 2'. But 8 − 4 = 4, not 2. Check at least two gaps. Then try division: 4 ÷ 2 = 2 and 8 ÷ 4 = 2. The rule is multiply by 2.

words.d: two times as much; 8 is double 4
a number you get by multiplying; 12 is a multiple of 3 because 3 × 4 = 12

look.title: Start at 1, Multiply by 2
look.prompt: What is term 10 of this pattern? What would term 10 be for 'start at 1, add 2' instead? Which is bigger, and by how much?

check.q: Rule: start at 5, multiply by 3. What is the 4th term?
check.why: 5, 15, 45, 135. Three multiplications by 3 after the start.

check.q: Pattern: 2, 6, 18, 54. What is the rule?
check.why: 6 ÷ 2 = 3, 18 ÷ 6 = 3 and 54 ÷ 18 = 3, so each term is 3 times the one before.

check.q: How can you tell a multiply pattern from an add pattern on a graph?
choices: Multiply patterns make a straight line
Multiply patterns curve upward, getting steeper
check.why: Add patterns rise the same amount each step and make a line. Multiply patterns rise more each step and make a curve.

lessons.title: Describing a Pattern's Features
lessons.mainIdea: Look beyond the rule: notice whether terms are odd or even, what digit they end in, and why that must happen.
reading: Once you have a pattern, describe what you notice. Rule: start at 3, add 3. Terms: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18. Notice that the terms switch between *odd* and *even*. Every term is a multiple of 3. Every other term is a multiple of 6. Each of these is a *feature* of the pattern. The rule does not say it out loud, but you can explain it. Adding 3 to an odd number gives an even number, and adding 3 to an even number gives an odd number. So the terms must alternate.

Rule: start at 4, add 4. Terms: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20. Every term is even. Why? 4 is even, and even plus even is always even, so the pattern can never reach an odd number. Rule: start at 5, add 10. Terms: 5, 15, 25, 35. Every term ends in 5. Why? Adding 10 changes the tens digit but never the ones digit.

Common mistake: describing only the first few terms. 'The terms are less than 20' is true for 4, 8, 12, 16 but false for 20. A good feature holds for every term, and you can say why. Another mistake: saying two patterns are the same because they share a few numbers. 'Add 3' and 'add 6' both contain 6 and 12, but they are different patterns with different rules.

words.d: something true about every term of a pattern, like 'all the terms are even'
a whole number that can be split into two equal whole parts: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 and so on
a whole number that is not even: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and so on

look.title: Odd or Even Forever
look.text: Rule: start at 7, add 2. Terms: 7, 9, 11, 13, 15. Every term is odd. Reason: 7 is odd, and adding 2, an even number, keeps a number odd. Now change the start. Rule: start at 6, add 2. Terms: 6, 8, 10, 12. Every term is even. Finally, rule: start at 6, add 5. Terms: 6, 11, 16, 21, 26.
look.prompt: Describe the odd-and-even feature of the 'start at 6, add 5' pattern, and explain why it happens.

check.q: Rule: start at 2, add 2. Which feature is true of every term?
check.why: 2 is even and adding 2 keeps it even, so the pattern 2, 4, 6, 8 and beyond is all even.

check.q: Rule: start at 10, add 10. What digit does every term end in?
check.why: 10, 20, 30, 40: adding 10 never changes the ones digit, which stays 0.

check.q: Rule: start at 1, add 3. Terms: 1, 4, 7, 10, 13. Which describes the odd-and-even feature?
check.why: Adding an odd number flips odd to even and back: 1 odd, 4 even, 7 odd, 10 even.

lessons.title: Maps and Coordinates
lessons.mainIdea: Real maps use coordinate ideas: a starting point, a direction across, a direction up, and distances you find by subtracting.
reading: Chicago's street addresses work like a coordinate plane. The origin is the corner of State Street and Madison Street downtown. State Street splits the city into east and west. Madison Street splits it into north and south. An *address* number grows as you move away from that corner. In most of the city, 800 address numbers equal about 1 mile. So an address of 1600 North is about 2 miles north of Madison Street.

Put a simple town on a *grid*. Each unit is 1 block. The school is at (2, 3), the library at (2, 9) and the pool at (8, 9). School to library: same x, so 9 − 3 = 6 blocks north. Library to pool: same y, so 8 − 2 = 6 blocks east. A walk from the school to the pool by way of the library is 6 + 6 = 12 blocks. Coordinates turn a map question into subtraction.

Grids show up in other places too. A spreadsheet names each *cell* by a column letter and a row number, like B4. A chessboard names each square the same way, from a1 to h8. In the game Battleship, you call out a letter and a number. Common mistake with real grids: forgetting which direction comes first. A chessboard reads column then row, just like (x, y). Check the labels before you count.

words.d: the number and street that name a place; in Chicago the numbers count away from State and Madison
a set of evenly spaced lines that cross, making squares you can count
one box in a spreadsheet, named by its column letter and row number

look.title: Chicago's Grid
look.text: Downtown Chicago's corner of State and Madison is the city's origin, its (0, 0). A shop is at 800 North on a north-south street, about 1 mile north of Madison. A friend lives at 2400 North, about 3 miles north. Both are north of the origin, so subtract the miles: 3 − 1 = 2 miles apart going north.
look.prompt: A park sits at 4000 North. About how many miles is it north of Madison Street? About how far is it from the shop at 800 North?

check.q: On a town grid, the bakery is at (4, 2) and the bank is at (4, 11). How many blocks apart are they?
check.why: Same x, so subtract the y-coordinates: 11 − 2 = 9 blocks.

check.q: In Chicago, about 800 address numbers make 1 mile. About how far from Madison Street is 3200 North?
A chessboard square is named e4. Which part comes first, like the x in (x, y)?
check.why: Chess names the column (across) first and the row (up) second, the same order as an ordered pair.

lessons.title: Shapes on the Grid
lessons.mainIdea: Plot the vertices, connect them, and use coordinates to find side lengths, missing corners and the perimeter.
reading: Plot A (2, 1), B (7, 1) and C (7, 4). Connect them and you have a right triangle. Side AB is horizontal: 7 − 2 = 5 units. Side BC is vertical: 4 − 1 = 3 units. The right angle is at B, the *vertex* where the horizontal and vertical sides meet. Coordinates let you find lengths without a ruler, as long as the sides run along grid lines.

Find a missing corner. Three corners of a rectangle are (1, 2), (6, 2) and (6, 5). The fourth corner must be straight above (1, 2) and straight left of (6, 5). So it shares x = 1 with the first point and y = 5 with the third: (1, 5). The rectangle is 6 − 1 = 5 units wide and 5 − 2 = 3 units tall. Its *perimeter*, the distance all the way around, is 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 units.

Common mistake: picking a missing corner because it looks about right. Use the shared coordinates instead. Another mistake: finding the width as 6 + 1 instead of 6 − 1. The width is a difference. Also remember that a slanted side, like the side from A to C in the triangle, cannot be found by subtracting coordinates. Only horizontal and vertical sides work that way.

words.d: a corner of a shape, where two sides meet; the plural is vertices
the distance all the way around a shape, found by adding the side lengths

look.title: The Garden Plot
look.text: A community garden in a city park is drawn on a grid where each unit is 1 meter. Its corners are (3, 2), (11, 2), (11, 8) and (3, 8). Width: 11 − 3 = 8 m. Height: 8 − 2 = 6 m. A fence goes all the way around: 8 + 6 + 8 + 6 = 28 m. Now the gardeners want more room.
look.prompt: They move the corners (11, 2) and (11, 8) so that x = 15 for both. What are the new width and the new fence length?

check.q: Three corners of a rectangle are (2, 3), (8, 3) and (8, 7). What is the fourth corner?
check.why: It shares x = 2 with (2, 3) and y = 7 with (8, 7), so it is (2, 7).

check.q: A rectangle has corners (0, 0), (9, 0), (9, 4) and (0, 4). What is its perimeter?
check.why: Width 9, height 4: 9 + 4 + 9 + 4 = 26. The number 36 is the area, not the perimeter.

check.q: Points (1, 1), (6, 1) and (6, 3) make a triangle. How long is the horizontal side?
check.why: From (1, 1) to (6, 1) the y is the same, so the length is 6 − 1 = 5.

review.q: Which point is 4 units right and 9 units up from the origin?
review.why: Right comes first and up comes second: (4, 9).

review.q: What is the distance from (3, 2) to (3, 12)?
review.why: Same x, so subtract the y-coordinates: 12 − 2 = 10.

review.q: Rule: start at 7, add 6. What is the 5th term?

review.why: 10 ÷ 5 = 2, 20 ÷ 10 = 2, 40 ÷ 20 = 2. The gaps 5, 10, 20 are not equal, so it is not an add rule.

review.q: Pattern A adds 5 from 0 and pattern B adds 10 from 0. At every step, B is
review.why: Step 1: 5 and 10. Step 3: 15 and 30. B is always 2 times A.

review.q: Which point lies on the y-axis?
review.why: A point on the y-axis has moved 0 to the right, so its x-coordinate is 0.

review.q: Three corners of a rectangle are (2, 2), (10, 2) and (10, 5). What is the fourth corner?
review.why: It shares x = 2 with (2, 2) and y = 5 with (10, 5).

review.q: Rule: start at 4, add 4. Which is true of every term?
choices: every term is a multiple of 3
review.why: 4 is even and even plus even is even, so 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 and beyond are all even.
